text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who is recovering from pneumonia in hospital, has become significantly more active and is working on documents, his doctors said on Sunday.

A medical bulletin released through the Kremlin said Yeltsin was in a stable condition with normal blood pressure, pulse and temperature. "To a significant degree, his activity has increased," the bulletin said.
Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov told Russian public television on Friday Yeltsin had pneumonia "of medium gravity" in both lungs.

Pneumonia, a serious infection or inflammation of the lungs, can affect one or both lungs. An infection of both lungs is considered more serious and difficult to treat. Doctors are using antibiotics to treat the condition.

The president's latest bout of ill health -- just two months after multiple heart bypass surgery -- has opened up a debate on whether Russia should alter its constitution to shift power from the president to the legislature.
At least one Moscow daily newspaper suggested because of his prolonged illnesses, it might be time for 65-year-old Yeltsin, post-Soviet Russia's first president, to step down.
"Regretfully, it is obvious that the president has no strength left to attend to affairs of state properly," the liberal daily Komsomolskaya Pravda said on Saturday.
Other newspapers have expressed doubts over Yeltsin's future ability to tackle festering problems.

Yeltsin's most vocal rival, his former security chief Alexander Lebed, has called for him to quit, and Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov has for months said that a sick Yeltsin is incapable of ruling the country.
Average Russians, many of whom see little direct connection between their daily lives and what happens in the Kremlin, appeared calmer about Yeltsin's latest illness.
Financial markets also shrugged off reports on his health, sending Russian markets into record territory on Friday. Some analysts said they expected more enthusiastic buying on Monday.

Mironov predicted the president would resume activities after a convalescence that "ideally" would continue until January 25 to 27. After that, the president should be able to resume full-time duties in the Kremlin, he said.
"I'm sure there will be no 50-50 situation -- the president spending half the time in the Kremlin and half in hospital," Sergei Mironov said on television.

"This is simply an episode, though a worrying one. Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin) is the sort of person who is always saying "Let's go, it's time to get going.' That was always the basis of his life's activity and work," he said.

Mironov had earlier said Yeltsin needed to remain in the hospital at least until the beginning of next week. The president, he said, was a reluctant and frustrated patient who had disregarded advice to enter hospital earlier for treatment.

The chairman of parliament's upper house said on Friday it was time to consider amending the 1993 constitution, drawn up after Yeltsin used tanks to put down a rebellion by parliament. Russia's Communists, the largest faction in parliament, also say they favour such changes.
